notes.urn:cts:latinLit:stoa0128b.stoa004.opp-l: Printed page numbers (340-344) embedded in the text are omitted. Ch. 1: the quoted words of Fastidiosus are an incomplete ablative-absolute clause in the source and are rendered as such. Ch. 3: the edition prints 'ex (forte in)'; 'in' is followed. 'spiritus Domini' read as 'Dominus' (the Lord), as sense requires. Ch. 4: the clause 'nec in spiritu quod dicitur separari ... cogitatur' is obscure and may be corrupt; rendered tentatively. Scanning errors corrected: 'separatas montes' read as 'mentes' (minds), 'non scit' as 'non facit', 'A- II.;' as 'Judaei' (Jews), 'Cat itas' as 'Caritas'. The citation 'Ephes. IV, 4' for 'the love of God has been poured out in our hearts' is as printed; the verse is Rom. 5:5. Scripture references given as the edition prints them (Vulgate numbering), with evident misprints corrected (e.g. Rom. 8:35, 38).

Ch. V: 'et eorum Deus a de longinquo' is corrupt; translated as Jer. 23:23 ('and not a God from afar'). 'in tuto carnis' read as 'in luto carnis' (mire of the flesh). 'non dico stultus, sed omnino sacrilegus' rendered loosely; sense is 'not merely a fool but an utter sacrilege'. Ch. VI: 'audeat indubitanter et asserere Trinitatem' seems to lack a word (e.g. 'divisam/separabilem'); supplied in brackets. In Heb. 1:3 'gratiae' read as 'gloriae'. Final clause 'aeternitas immensitatem, aeternitatem immensitas aequalem' is elliptical. Many scripture references in the edition are garbled (e.g. 'Isai. II, 6' for 9:6, 'Isai. VII, 44' for 7:14); corrected in translation.

Ch. XIV: the edition reads 'Quomodo igitur... habere potuit', which does not fit the following 'ita'; translated as 'Just as... could not have', following the evident sense (likely 'non potuit'). The stray 'a' after 'potuit' is taken as a footnote mark. Ch. XI: 'naturam vero secundum carnem' is read as 'nativitatem', which the sense requires. In the Ps. and Isa. references the edition's numbering is kept as printed.

Ch. XVII end: 'Quid autem accepimus? Domini Verbum et Deum apud quem erat Verbum, non Patrem et Filium' appears corrupt; translated as if 'Dominum Verbum, et non Deum apud quem erat Verbum; non Patrem, sed Filium', which the argument requires. Ch. XVII: 'augurio' ('as a sign of') is odd and may be corrupt. Ch. XVIII: 'Nos ergo Patra' read as 'Non ergo Patris'; 'sicut eam accepit Filius, sic accepit Pater' contradicts the argument (common working = making, not taking up); translated as 'made', reading 'fecit'. Scripture references corrected where the edition's figures are garbled (Wis. 9:17; 1 Cor. 2:12; 1 Cor. 9:22).

In ch. XX 'inivisus' is taken as 'indivisus' (undivided); 'invisus' or 'invisibilis' would also be possible readings. The edition cites 1 Cor. 15:5 for the creed quotation; the passage is 1 Cor. 15:3-4.
Evident scanning errors read as: 'Quid autem' for 'Quid ait tem', 'sancta' for 'Macta', 'opere Trinitatis' for 'operi Trinitatis' (by the work of the Trinity), 'salvus' for 'salvum'.

nodes.text: SAINT FULGENTIUS, AGAINST THE SERMON OF FASTIDIOSUS THE ARIAN, TO VICTOR: ONE BOOK.
CHAPTER ONE.

When, dearest son Victor, I was reading over your letter, which carries the most sweet fragrance of faith and charity, with complete delight and eagerness of mind, I found attached to it the sermon of Fastidiosus, which you had sent me to refute. When I had read it through, I grieved for him as lost as much as I was driven to shudder at him as a blasphemer. We know that after [embracing] the Christian faith, after the profession of a monk, after the honour of the priesthood, which he took up in the sight of men but did not hold before the Lord, he turned aside from the way of truth and wholly forgot his own redemption, became a slave of fornication and lust, and as a result rejected the service of the divine majesty. That is why, having turned from a catholic into a heretic, and bringing forth evil things out of the evil treasure of his heart, he not undeservedly vomits up that sermon against the right faith and against catholic truth, drunk on the poison of impiety, since he rejected the bread of life and, as the sign of his own name shows, disdainfully threw away the wholesome food of the true faith. In that profane sermon, calling us Homousians, as the Arians are accustomed to name us, he set down these words: "The Homousians," he says, "asserting that the Trinity is inseparable and indivisible, that the Son was not less than the Father, and that the unbegotten Father is not the maker of his Son." Note, I beg you, that in these words of Fastidiosus some things are so wrongly put that they can never rightly be asserted, while others are said by him impiously in such a way that they can also rightly, provided only that piety is present, be both said and heard. For that point on which he thought we should be refuted, namely that we call the Trinity inseparable and indivisible, he put forward so wrongly and impiously that no one could put it forward rightly. For who does not see with what great impiety the Trinity is asserted by the Arians to be separable? The blessed Apostle says of us: "Who will separate us from the love of Christ? Tribulation, or distress, or danger, or famine, or persecution, or the sword?" (Rom. 8:35). And a little later: "I am certain that neither death, nor life, nor angels, nor principalities, nor things present, nor things to come, nor powers, nor height, nor depth, nor any other creature will be able to separate us from the love of God, which is in Christ Jesus our Lord" (ibid., 38).
CHAPTER II.

Since, then, the blessed Apostle is confident that through the grace of God we cannot be separated from his love, how do those not perceive that they are bound in the deadly snare of impiety who do not hesitate to preach that the holy Trinity is separated, when they cannot show that its works are in any respect separable? For in what the evangelist says of the Son, "All things were made through him, and without him nothing was made" (John 1:3); and in what blessed David sings, "How magnified are your works, O Lord! You have made all things in wisdom" (Ps. 103:24); and since the blessed Apostle professes Christ to be the power of God and the wisdom of God, of whom it is said, "For in him were founded all things in heaven and on earth, visible and invisible, whether Thrones, or Dominions, or Principalities, or Powers; all things were created through him and in him" (Col. 1:16): it is plain that all the works of the Father are the same as the works of the Son, and the same as the works of the Holy Spirit. For the holy Trinity works inseparably: there is no work which the Father has done and the Son has not done, or which the Son has done and the Holy Spirit has not done. For it is written: "By the Word of the Lord the heavens were made firm, and all their power by the Spirit of his mouth" (Ps. 32:6). Concerning the wisdom too which we say was created in the angels, we read it written in the book of Ecclesiasticus: "Wisdom was created before all things, and the understanding of prudence from eternity" (Ecclus. 1:4). To show that the angels too were made by the Word of God, through whom all things were made, holy Scripture straightway added: "The fountain of wisdom is the Word of God, and her ways are the eternal commandments" (ibid., 5). And a little later, to show that the angels belong to the works of the Holy Spirit, it says this: "There is one most high Creator, almighty, a powerful King, and greatly to be feared, sitting upon her throne and ruling. God created her by the Holy Spirit" (ibid., 8). What then will be denied to have been made by the Holy Spirit, by whom the power of the heavens is read to have been made firm, and whose work created wisdom is declared to be? For when the blessed Apostle was speaking of the divine gifts which God bestows on his Church, and had said, "Now there are divisions of graces, but the same Spirit; and there are divisions of ministries, but the same God, who works all things in all" (1 Cor. 12:4), then, having listed the diversity of heavenly gifts, he went on: "All these things one and the same Spirit works, dividing to each as he wills" (ibid., 11). And what in all the creatures, in which wisdom "reaches mightily from end to end and orders all things sweetly" (Wis. 8:1), could be found foreign to the working of the Holy Spirit, when Christ, who is the power and wisdom of God, declares that he casts out demons by the Spirit of God? For he himself said: "But if I cast out demons by the Spirit of God, then the kingdom of God has come upon you" (Matt. 12:28). How then does Fastidiosus deny that the Trinity is inseparable, when no Christian dares to deny that the works of the Trinity are the same and inseparable in all creatures? For the one God, namely the Father, and the Son, and the Holy Spirit, works inseparably. For the Only-begotten of God declares that his works are the same as those of his Father, saying: "For whatever the Father does, these same things the Son also does likewise" (John 5:19). And yet what the Son does, he does in the Holy Spirit, in whom he casts out demons.
CHAPTER III.

But lest, because we have said that the Son too does in the Holy Spirit whatever he does, the Arians should wish to raise some question of difference, thinking that the one in whom something is done ought to be taken as less than the one who does it, let them hear our Saviour resisting this perversity in every way when he says: "But he who does the truth comes to the light, so that his works may be made manifest, that they have been done in God" (John 3:21). Here let the Arians choose how they wish to take the name "God": as the Father, or the Son, or the Holy Spirit? If they think it should be taken as the Father, in whom good works are done by men, they themselves destroy the objection they blasphemously raise against the person of the Holy Spirit. For they will not dare to call the Father less, to whom they refuse to proclaim the Son equal according to divinity. And so, since man does good works in the Father, and Christ casts out demons in the Holy Spirit, let them recognise the equality of the Father and the Holy Spirit. But if they say that the Son is to be understood here, then, since good works are done in the Son and in the Holy Spirit, not only are they compelled to confess that the Son and the Holy Spirit are equal, but they will also confess that the works of the Father, and the Son, and the Holy Spirit are the same and inseparable: for "one and the same Spirit works all things" (1 Cor. 12:11), as the blessed Apostle testifies. But if the Arians judge it to be the Holy Spirit, then from this passage they must be compelled to confess that the Holy Spirit is God. For the Lord did not say, "He who does the truth, so that his works may be made manifest, that they have been done in the Holy Spirit," but "that they have been done in God": [works] which we say are done not in the Father alone, nor in the Son alone, nor in the Holy Spirit alone, but we confess that truth is done by man in the holy Trinity itself, which is one God, in whom blessed David indicates that valour is done by the faithful, saying: "In the Lord we shall do valiantly, and he will bring to nothing those who afflict us" (Ps. 59:14). For he is the one God of whom the blessed Apostle says: "For from him and in him are all things: to him be glory for ever" (Rom. 11:36).
CHAPTER IV.

How then is the holy Trinity called separable by the impious, when it works inseparably, by whom, as far as can be understood, what it means to be separated is not conceived even in spirit, as the truth of the matter demands? For from our God, that is, from the holy Trinity itself, nothing can be separated in place, because the same God, supreme, true and good, just as he made all things, so in his immensity contains and fills all things. He is not bodily, nor in a place, and therefore not even bodily things can be separated from God in place; because every body is in a place, and without God there is no place. For God is contained by no place in such a way that he himself contains every place; in him there is no mass, and his power is immeasurable. Since, then, bodies, which cannot exist without place, cannot be separated from God in place, without doubt neither are the spirits which God created separated from God in place. For in whatever place any spirit that God created may be, there God is: and although he is not in evil spirits by grace, by which he bestows holy life and blessedness on whom he wills, yet by his natural power he is always in all his creatures in such a way that no creature, or particle of a creature, can be found in which God is not by his power. That nature, therefore, can be separated from God which could or can be subject to sin. Nor is there any other thing that can depart from God except a substance which can or could sin by its own will. For Isaiah says: "Behold, the hand of the Lord is not shortened, that it cannot save, nor is his ear dulled, that it cannot hear; but your iniquities divide between you and your God" (Isa. 59:1-2). In the book of Wisdom too it is shown that men are separated from God not by places, but by depraved thoughts and wicked deeds. For there it is said: "For perverse thoughts separate from God. And proven power rebukes the foolish: because wisdom will not enter a malicious soul, nor dwell in a heart subject to sins; for the holy Spirit of discipline will flee deceit, and will withdraw himself from thoughts that are without understanding" (Wis. 1:3-5). Here who does not see the Trinity intimated by the properties of the persons? For it is said that perverse thoughts separate from God, by which name the person of God the Father is recognised. Then it is added that wisdom will not enter a malicious soul, by which name Christ is shown, whom Paul calls the power of God and the wisdom of God. Then it is said that the Holy Spirit will flee deceit and will withdraw himself from thoughts that are without understanding. But lest anyone should think that any wicked or impious people could be separated in place from this holy Trinity, which is the one, true and good God, a little later Scripture speaks thus: "For the Spirit of wisdom is kind, and will not free the evil-speaker from his lips, since God is witness of his reins, and the true examiner of his heart, and the hearer of his tongue. For the Spirit of the Lord has filled the whole world" (ibid., 6-7). And so the divine utterances do not cease to proclaim the immensity of the holy Trinity. This blessed David certainly knew most surely, and therefore he said: "Where shall I go from your Spirit, and where shall I flee from your face? If I ascend into heaven, you are there; if I descend into hell, you are present" (Ps. 138:7-8). Of Wisdom too, that is, the Son of God, Scripture says that it "reaches from end to end, and orders all things sweetly" (Wis. 8:1). Since, therefore, nothing is separated in place from the holy Trinity, which is everywhere whole, but, as we have already said, only iniquities and perverse thoughts separate from God, whoever tries to assert that the Trinity is separable must say that either the Father or the Son or the Holy Spirit can by nature be subject to depraved thoughts and iniquities. But who would entangle himself in the snare of so great an impiety as to suspect any separation in that Trinity where there is a natural unity, when, through grace received, as we have shown above, the faithful Paul is confident that he can in no way be separated from the love of God which is in Christ Jesus our Lord? Now the blessed apostle John confirms both that love is from God and that love is God, in these words: "Beloved, let us love one another, because love is from God, and everyone who loves is from God" (1 John 4:7); and, "God is love" (ibid., 16). It certainly cannot be separated from itself, because it is inseparable. For since it not only holds men, who can be separated from one another, inseparable, but makes out of many hearts and souls one heart and one soul, what madness is it to call love itself separable, which is accustomed to join separated minds in inseparable affection? Hence indeed Paul said: "For though I am absent in body, yet I am with you in spirit, rejoicing and seeing your order" (Col. 2:5). And in the Acts of the Apostles it is written that "the multitude of believers had one heart and soul" (Acts 4:32); which certainly nothing does but the spirit of faith and love. For "the love of God has been poured out in our hearts" (Ephes. 4:4). And through that same Spirit it comes about that all believers, as the Apostle says, are one body and one spirit. Hence he says in another place: "For in one spirit we were all baptised into one body, whether Jews or Gentiles, whether slaves or free, and we have all been given to drink in one spirit" (1 Cor. 12:13). And the only-begotten Son of God commanded with his own mouth that all nations be baptised in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit,
CHAPTER V.

When, therefore, baptism is given in the name of the Trinity, it causes all the faithful to be baptised into one body, so that from this all are made one body, as the blessed Apostle says, that "we are one body in Christ, and individually members one of another" (Rom. 12:5). The multitude of believers also had one heart and soul through love, which "has been poured out in our hearts through the Holy Spirit, who has been given to us". It is plainly evident with what great impiety the Trinity itself is called separable, since in fact any creature whatever is separated from God not by place, not by time, but by its iniquities alone. Hence it is that God says of certain people: "This people honours me with their lips, but their heart is far from me" (Matt. 15:8). And yet he himself says: "I am a God who draws near, and not a God from afar. If a man has hidden himself, shall I not see him? Do I not fill heaven and earth?" (Jer. 23:23-24). Yet David himself says: "Behold, those who distance themselves from you shall perish" (Ps. 72:27). And to show what it is to distance oneself from God, he added: "You have destroyed all who commit fornication away from you" (ibid.). It is therefore with the heart that one withdraws from God, to whom one also draws near with the heart. For it is evident that God is wholly everywhere, but is in no way contained by place. For God is spirit, the creator indeed, not created, the unchangeable maker of all bodies and all spirits, eternal, immeasurable, just and good. He never departs, by the immeasurability of his nature, from any of the things which he has made. For it cannot be that God himself, by his power, should be absent from any thing which has from God that it exists. And yet, through the mercy and judgement which the Church does not cease to sing to him (Ps. 100:1), he is not unfittingly said both to be present to the faithful and to be far away from the unfaithful. For as regards nature: since the holy Trinity alone, that is, the one God, who is Father, and Son, and Holy Spirit, made all that is created, whether bodily or spiritual, by one will, one operation, one power, one benevolence, and one omnipotence; just as the Father fills the whole creation, by power, that is, not by bulk, so the Son fills the whole, so the Holy Spirit fills the whole. For the Trinity does not fill the whole creation in such a way that the Father fills a part, the Son a part, the Holy Spirit a part, and yet the whole is not filled by the Father alone, nor by the Son alone, nor by the Holy Spirit alone. For who would dare to think thus of the Trinity, that is, of the one God, I do not say a fool, but anyone at all short of a sacrilegious man; since the power and divinity of God must necessarily be as immeasurable by nature as it is everlasting by nature? But men given over to carnal senses cannot think even of God himself except carnally. And they suppose that the Father, and the Son, and the Holy Spirit can be separated from one another just as men are separated from each other; who, just as they are distinguished by the measure and size of each one's body, must necessarily also be set apart by places. But such people, while they roll their souls in the mire of the flesh, with phantasms of their own creating, and weighed down by the burden of vanity, the more they dwell on the thought of those things which present bodily bulk to bodily eyes, the less they are able to climb up to understanding the Godhead. Nor do they heed that the Lord God commands through holy Isaiah that we should not wish to think of him as we think of creatures, which we know were made by him; since he himself does not think as we men think. Hence Isaiah says: "For my thoughts are not your thoughts, nor are my ways your ways, says the Lord: for as the heavens are exalted above the earth, so are my ways exalted above your ways, and my thoughts above your thoughts" (Isa. 55:8-9).
CHAPTER VI.

Thus God the Father, and his Word, and the Holy Spirit, that is, the holy Trinity, the only, one, true and good God, just as there is in him no thought which varies with the turning of time (for he did not, as men do, think one way before he made the world, and think another way after he made the world, or will think another way after the form of this world has passed away; because "the counsel of the Lord abides for ever" [Ps. 32:11]), so is he inseparable as he is unchangeable. For the Trinity, the one God, is neither a body nor a created spirit; because a body is enclosed by place, and every spirit that is created is bounded by the measure of its own nature. But the Trinity, the one God, just as he is eternal, and no times are coeternal with him, so is he immeasurable, whom no creature can enclose; and because immeasurable, wholly everywhere; because he is neither contained by place, nor stretched out or contracted by space. God, then, is wisdom, God is truth, God is love. This is the Father, this the Son, this the Holy Spirit, this the Trinity itself, which is the one, true and good God. If anyone, therefore, can show that there is some division either in wisdom, or in truth, or in love, let him dare also to assert without hesitation [the division of] the Trinity. But if neither wisdom, nor truth, nor love is divided in any way, then from this the Trinity is certainly recognised to be indivisible and inseparable. It is evident, therefore, how great was the impiety of Fastidiosus, by which he thought we were altogether to be blamed because we confess the Trinity to be inseparable and undivided: since indeed, as the preceding discussion has shown (which not only reason but also an ample store of divine testimonies has confirmed), neither can the immeasurable nature of the Trinity be contained by place, nor can any person in the Trinity be subject to sin: because the Trinity itself is by nature of eternal, perfect and unchangeable justice. Heretical depravity, indeed, wickedly strives to assert that the Son is lesser; but catholic truth, keeping piety, confesses him equal. For the heretics, thinking of the incorporeal divinity only in a bodily way, when they say that the Son is lesser according to nature, under the guise of the Christian name which they falsely put forward, entangle themselves in the unspeakable crime of idolatry. For what is it to speak of a greater god and a lesser god in the individual persons, except to set up idols of different kind and different power, not on walls but, what is worse, in hearts? For from this the Arians plainly show that they worship two gods, while they deny that the Son is equal to the Father; and when they assert that he is lesser, not by the assumption of flesh (which the truth of the faith holds), but in the nature of the immeasurable divinity, although it has been said of him, who is the wisdom of God, that he is "the brightness of eternal light" (Wis. 7:26). Of whom it is said in the Epistle to the Hebrews: "Who, being the splendour of glory, and the image of his substance" (Heb. 1:3). Let them attend, then, to the brightness of eternal light, and recognise that, just as that light is eternal and immeasurable, so it has its brightness too neither later by nature in any way, nor lesser; but eternity has immeasurability equal to it, and immeasurability eternity.
CHAPTER VII.

The Christian faith, therefore, which knows the Only-begotten God both as alone born from the nature of the Father and as created from the Virgin Mary, recognising that each substance truly remains in him, so confesses him, truly [born] from God the Father, to be equal to the Father, that without the crime of falsehood and impiety it proclaims him also lesser. For since he has one natural divinity with the Father, and one natural humanity with his mother, the Son is equal to the Father in that respect in which he is true God from the Father, and the Father is greater than the Son in that respect in which the Only-begotten God himself is true man. This, then, is the true faith, this the holy piety, this the Christian belief: in one and the same Son of God both to believe the nature of the Father's divinity, and not to deny the substance of the mother's humanity; neither to believe the divinity of the Son different from the divinity of God the Father, nor [to believe] the humanity of the Son separated from the humanity of the Virgin who bore him, but to believe in the same true God the true and whole humanity of our kind, and in the same true and whole man to believe the true and full Godhead of the Father's nature. For he who denies the unity of the Father's substance in the Son is defiled by the Arian impiety; he who denies the reality of the flesh in the Only-begotten God is profaned by the crime of the Manichaean plague; and he who denies in the same Son of God a human, that is, a rational soul, is straightway stained by the sacrilege of the Apollinarists.
CHAPTER VIII.

Wherefore, when the reality of the Father's and the mother's nature in the Only-begotten God is believed in its fullness, and the natural property of the twofold substance is preserved in the one person of Christ, the Son is piously and truly said to be both equal to the Father and lesser, piously and truly he is proclaimed coeternal and later, piously and truly he is asserted to be both always born and born in time, both always unchangeable and changed in time. And so the Son is equal to the Father, because he always has this from the Father. He is also lesser than the Father, because he received this in time from the Virgin. Wherefore, just as the Son is piously said to be equal to the Father when the humanity in him, by which he is lesser than the Father, is not being considered, so the same Son is impiously said to be lesser when the unity and equality of divinity with the Father is denied to be in him by nature. We say, therefore, that the Son is by nature equal, and we say that he is lesser. We say that according to the form of God he was born equal, but according to the form of a servant he was made lesser in condition. We say he is equal to the Father, in that we know him to be born without beginning from the Father; we say he is also lesser, because "when the fullness of time came, God sent his Son, made from a mother, made under the law" (Gal. 4:4). Accordingly, just as we proclaim without hesitation that he was born, so indeed we proclaim also that he was made. For we say that he was born without beginning from the heart of the Father, we say that he was made in time by the work of the Trinity. For the Father both begot his own proper Son from his own nature, and made him from the nature of the virgin. But whatever he made, he made with the Son and the Holy Spirit working together. The Father alone, then, begot his Son, but did not alone make him. For in the Only-begotten Son there is the eternal generation of the Father alone, and in the same Son as made there is the one operation of the whole Trinity. For the Only-begotten God, the creator of man, was created man, and the same one who made woman from man was made man from woman. Hence it is evident that the testimonies which Fastidiosus impiously brought forward from the Gospel and from the Acts of the Apostles, and from Solomon, do not take away from the Son the unity of the Father's nature, but show the mystery of the divine incarnation. Knowing this most certainly, John the Baptist said: "This is he of whom I said: After me comes one who was made before me" (John 1:15). Proclaiming the truth of this mystery, the apostle Peter says: "Most certainly, therefore, let all the house of Israel know that God has made him both God and Christ, this Jesus whom you crucified" (Acts 2:36). Fittingly indeed did he say "made" of the one whom he proclaims crucified; for the Only-begotten God, incomprehensible and immortal, made by no one, and the eternal maker of all things, deigned to become Christ by his own work, so that he could be crucified by the work of the Jews; because the cross could in no way have borne the Redeemer of the world when he was handed over, had not the womb of a virgin brought forth the maker of the world when conceived. He himself, therefore, indicating also through Solomon the truth of his generation and his creation, said: "The Lord created me at the beginning of his ways, in his work" (Prov. 8:22). But before he said this, he set first a clear indication of his future incarnation, saying: "If I declare to you the things that happen daily, I will recall the things that are from the age" (ibid. 21, according to the Septuagint). Then, enumerating, he added: "The Lord created me at the beginning of his ways, in his work." This creation indeed is from the age, not before the age. For afterwards he says, "Before the ages he established me"; and shortly after: "Before all the hills he begot me." Here, in saying "before the ages" and "before all the hills", he wished the eternity of the divine birth to be understood. Both before the age and after the age there is eternity. And thus the eternity of the Son of God before the age has no beginning, just as his eternity after the age has no end. Thus, then, putting the past tense for the future tense, Wisdom says, "The Lord created me," in place of "he will create me"; and so he spoke as if done of what was indeed yet to be done: just as he said through blessed David: "They dug my hands and my feet: they numbered all my bones. And they considered and gazed upon me. They divided my garments among them, and upon my garment they cast lots" (Ps. 21:17-19). So, by saying "The Lord created me," he showed how he was to be made. And by saying "They dug my hands and my feet," he showed how he was to be crucified. Just as this was indeed still to come which the Son of God sang through David of his passion as if done, so that was still to come which he who is the wisdom of God prophesied through Solomon of his incarnation as if done. For Solomon himself says a little earlier: "Wisdom has built a house for herself, and set beneath it seven pillars" (Prov. 9:1), which pertains to the origin of the Lord's incarnation. Isaiah too speaks of Christ's passion in such a way that he speaks of what he prophesies as future as if it were past. For he says of Christ: "He was led like a sheep to the slaughter, and like a lamb voiceless before its shearer, so he did not open his mouth" (Isa. 53:7). For he also foretells the very birth of the Only-begotten God according to the flesh from the Virgin, not only sometimes as future, but sometimes speaks of it as past. Thus in one place he says: "Behold, a virgin shall conceive in the womb, and bear a son" (Isa. 7:14). Again in another place, indicating it as done and accomplished, he says: "A child has been born to us, and a son has been given to us" (Isa. 9:6). Who then does not see that all that was said through the prophets about the humanity and passion of the Only-begotten God was at that time as truly in the future as it is now truly in the past? But to show the unchangeableness of the divine counsel, it came about that prophetic Scripture spoke in word as past what was awaited as future in deed. For God, of whom the prophet here says, "Who made the things that are to come" (Isa. 45:11, according to the Septuagint), wished to narrate as done the things that were to be done, because the things that happen changeably in time he has made firm by the unchangeable eternity of his disposition. And so even in those things in which the effect of the work does not yet exist, the disposition of the creator remains firm in eternity. Thus, then, the Son of God, since he was to be created by his own work, said that he had been created, just as, when he was to be crucified, he did not hesitate to say that he had been crucified.
CHAPTER IX.

But Fastidiosus, still raving with perverse heart and sacrilegious mouth, wished to assert from this that the Son is separated from the Father and the Holy Spirit: that it is agreed that he alone entered the bridal chamber of the virginal womb, of which it is said in the book of Psalms: "And he, like a bridegroom coming forth from his bridal chamber" (Ps. 18:6). Then, wishing to strengthen the opinion of his perversity, he did not hesitate to assert this blasphemy too, saying that the Trinity, which it is agreed is in no way divided, could in no way separate itself. So then, did the whole Trinity take on flesh, did the whole Trinity feel the injury of the sufferings, did the whole Trinity lie in the tomb, did the whole Trinity go down into hell, did the whole Trinity rise from the dead on the third day, did the whole Trinity ascend into heaven on the fortieth day? At whose right hand does the whole Trinity sit, or what Spirit did the whole Trinity send upon the apostles on the day of Pentecost, or to what God could the whole Trinity say on the cross, "My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?", or to what Father did the whole Trinity say, "Father, into your hands I commend my spirit"? Let them declare it, if they can. But if they cannot say it, they who contend that the Trinity is inseparable destroy themselves with their own darts.
CHAPTER X.

Thus far the words of Fastidiosus in that profane sermon are directed against the catholic faith. In it, however, apart from the things he blasphemed to the insult of the holy Trinity, almost everything, whether preceding or following, the most wicked man appropriated from the sayings of others. Indeed, everything that he set down against the Donatists he stole from two letters, in which, when we, placed in exile in Sardinia, had to reply on behalf of all to the devout daughter of the Church Stephania against the Pelagians and the Donatists, those things are found inserted in the very order of words in which this same most wicked man fraudulently set them down under his own name. And so that you might not lack knowledge of this matter, I have had the two letters which the aforesaid Stephania sent to us, and those which we wrote back to her, appended to this little work, so that you may recognise that in that sermon only those things were Fastidiosus's with which, leaping forth with blind heart to the insult of the holy Trinity itself, he tried to attack the catholic truth.
CHAPTER XI.

Now therefore, with the Lord's help, I answer his blasphemies. The whole Trinity did not take on flesh, nor did the whole Trinity feel the injuries of the sufferings, nor did the whole Trinity lie in the tomb, nor did the whole Trinity go down into hell, nor did the whole Trinity rise from the dead on the third day, nor [any] other things there may be which are shown, in that mystery of the incarnation, to belong to the person of the Son alone. For these charges, full of falsehood and perversity, which Fastidiosus brought against the catholic truth, can truly be brought only against the Sabellians, that is, the Patripassians; and under them those men, confined and convicted, truly fail, who contend that the holy Trinity has, as one nature, so one person. There their perversity consequently hurls them into this absurdity, that they in no way believe in the divine birth [of the Son], yet consequently assign to the Father the birth according to the flesh, as well as the passion and death, the resurrection from the underworld, the ascension into heaven, and all those things which in the mystery of the incarnation belong to the person of the one Son. But the catholic Church, divinely inspired, holding the truth of the faith, just as it knows how to assert one nature of the holy Trinity, so most carefully assigns to each person what is its own. The Son of God, then, about to redeem us in mercy, is rightly believed to have alone taken [flesh] on, because he did not take up human nature in such a way that one nature of divinity and flesh came to be in him. For in Christ the Godhead could not be the same thing as the flesh, because, each nature keeping its own property, it could not happen that either of them should cease to be, or should pass into the other by a complete abolition. If that happened, it would rightly be said that flesh was taken up by the whole Trinity, since the Son would turn his flesh into that divinity which we profess remains common to him with the Father and the Holy Spirit.
CHAPTER XII.

But now, since we say that in Christ there is one nature divine and another human, for that reason we certainly believe and confess that the human nature, that is, flesh and a rational soul, was taken up not by the whole Trinity but by the Son alone. For the Only-begotten God took up flesh and soul into unity of person, not into unity of nature, because the person of the Son is certainly not the same as that of the Father or of the Holy Spirit. The unity of person, then, while the property of each substance remains, just as it did not make the person in Christ double, so it did not make the taking up of human nature common to the holy Trinity. For the Son of God does not have, as one and common nature with the Father and the Holy Spirit, so also one and common person.
CHAPTER XIII.

It is therefore proper to the Son alone to have taken on in mercy the form of a servant. For that taking on of the servile form belonged to the person of God the Word (another reading: true), [a form] which did not pass into the divine nature by confusion. Therefore the taking on of that servile form, according to which the Son of God, who is Lord of all things and in whom dwells all the fullness of the Godhead, became true and full man, took nothing from him of the divine fullness, removed nothing of his lordship, because in that one person the divine and human nature remained without confusion. Hence it is that in one and the same Christ both the reality of the human nature shone forth, and the unchangeableness of the divine nature remained eternal. For what he had by nature in eternity was neither in any way diminished in him nor changed through what he received in time. For he became a servant in outward condition, but did not cease to be by nature Lord of all things. And he became poor according to the flesh; nevertheless he remained most rich according to the divinity. Hence it is that the blessed Apostle asserts that Christians are made rich by poverty, saying: "You know the grace of our Lord Jesus Christ, that for our sake he became needy when he was rich, so that by his poverty you might be rich" (2 Cor. 8:9). But he would in no way make us rich by his poverty if, having become poor, he did not have in himself the riches of his natural divinity. He became poor, then, according to the form of a servant; he remained rich according to the form of God. So the poverty of the servile form is not common to him with the Father and the Holy Spirit, because after the poverty of human nature was taken up into unity of person, the divine substance remained rich in him. And what was the poverty of the rich Son of God, if not our weakness and our mortality? Whatever the Only-begotten God endured in weakness and death according to the flesh, the divinity did not feel. For God sent his Son in the likeness of sinful flesh (Rom. 8:3), in whom there was true flesh but no pollution of sin. So the likeness of sinful flesh was in the flesh of Christ, though it was not the flesh of sin, in this: that it was weak, that it was passible and mortal, that it was liable to wounds and subject to pain. Yet all these things were common to the divinity and humanity of Christ not substantially but personally. But the person of Christ is wholly distinguished from the person of the Father and of the Holy Spirit. This one person of divinity and humanity in Christ so remains that it neither allows one nature to be separated from the other, nor permits the two to be confused. Christ, therefore, who is the way, the truth, and the true life, is the way for us because he had true weakness in the reality of the flesh; and he is true life for us because true power remained in his true divinity. Distinguishing this, the Apostle says: "For although he was crucified out of weakness, yet he lives by the power of God" (2 Cor. 13:4).
CHAPTER XIV.

In one and the same Christ, then, just as the weakness of human flesh could neither give nor give back life to itself, because that power of laying down the soul and taking it up was not from human weakness but from divine power, so the eternity of divine power, to which it is proper by nature to live unchangeably and unfailingly, could feel nothing of weakness or death on the cross. So the Only-begotten Son of God is recognised as true God born of the Father and true man made of a mother in this, that he both showed signs of weakness in the reality of the flesh and displayed proofs of power in the reality of the divinity; showing, that is, in the unity of person, that one thing is by nature common to him with us, another with the Father and the Holy Spirit. For Christ has with us a natural communion of soul and flesh; but with the Father and the Holy Spirit he has a natural communion of Godhead. Just as, therefore, the Son of God could not have the things of the flesh in common with the Father and the Holy Spirit, since he in no way confuses his flesh with his divinity, so it does not prejudice the catholic faith that we believe our nature was taken up into unity of person by the Only-begotten Saviour, while we confess that the substance of the holy Trinity remains one. For the whole Trinity made that humanity of the Son, but the whole Trinity did not take it up as the whole Trinity made it, because the person which is not common to the Son with the Father and the Holy Spirit is itself in Christ the one [person] of divinity and flesh. And where any distinction, whether of persons or of substances, is found, whatever is found in common working is not always referred to common taking up. Because this seems obscure when it is put forward in words alone, it is better that ease of understanding be provided by a suitable example, so far as the matter permits.
CHAPTER XV.

There is indeed a likeness readily available to the faithful for understanding, which God set in his own likeness. And this image is the human mind. For we read that the Lord said: "Let us make man in our image and likeness" (Gen. 1:26). In this saying the Arian heretics are much to be pitied, who read the holy Scriptures and do not understand them; and, confounded by blindness of heart, they do not acknowledge the natural unity in the holy Trinity, in which they distinguish in their preaching the persons of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit. Yet in that testimony which we set out above, the Trinity itself, which is the one, true and good God, both shows the unity of its divinity and clearly gives evidence of three persons. For he said, "Let us make man in our image and likeness," so that the unity of substance in three persons should not be denied; and he did not say, "I will make man in my image and likeness," so that only one person should not be believed to be in that divine nature. Instead he soundly mixed the plural with the singular number, and when we read God saying, "Let us make man in our image and likeness," what we say is singular in the nature we define as plural in the persons. And so this image, that is, the inner man, is found to have by nature three things within it: memory, understanding, and will. Memory, then, is the power of the soul by which we remember. Understanding is that by which we turn over in thought what we have taken in by memory. Will is that by which we either seek something or avoid it: that is, by which we are found either to love something or to hate it. These three, then, although they do not have their own persons in a man, are nevertheless distinct from one another; and so in these three there is one person of one man and one substance of the human mind, yet in the very nature of the rational soul, in which the image of God is known to be, we find memory to be one thing, understanding another, and will likewise another. For although we can think of, love or hate nothing that we do not hold in memory, since what forgetfulness has taken away from the heart, thought or will cannot find there in any way, still, to recognise the distinction of memory, thought and will: we often remember what we neither turn over in thought nor seek with the will; again, we think of some things which we do not love. Our thought, therefore, which is born and formed in the memory, is fittingly called an inner word. For what is thought but inward speech? Hence it is written: "What you say in your hearts, be sorry for also on your beds" (Ps. 4:5). And in the Gospel too, when the Lord Jesus had said to the paralytic whom he healed, "Your sins are forgiven you" (Luke 5:20), Luke the evangelist added: "And the scribes and Pharisees began to think, saying: Who is this who speaks blasphemy? Who can forgive sins but God alone? But when Jesus knew their thoughts, he answered and said to them: Why do you think evil things in your hearts?" (ibid. 21, 22). And what Luke said, "The scribes and Pharisees began to think, saying," Matthew puts thus: "And behold, some of the scribes said within themselves: He blasphemes. And when Jesus saw their thoughts, he said: Why do you think evil things in your hearts?" (Matt. 9:3, 4). In the book of Wisdom also it is said of certain people: "They said within themselves, thinking not rightly" (Wis. 2:1). It is clear, then, that to think is to speak within oneself. There, then, thinking takes place invisibly. So without the sound of a bodily voice each one says what he thinks, which, however, he does not bring to another's hearing except by bodily speech.
CHAPTER XVI.

So that word which is born from the memory cannot, according to that nature alone by which it is found to be born from the memory, be brought to the ears of any man without a bodily voice. Therefore, so that it may be brought forth to others, it is clothed in the garment of a bodily voice. To this word a bodily voice from the mouth is joined. And so it comes about that the word which was wholly in the mind spiritually both comes to others through the bodily voice and does not withdraw from the mind, from which and in which it spiritually remains. For it must remain wholly in the mind even when it is wholly uttered in the voice. Yet we cannot say that that utterance of the word alone does not come about from memory or from will. For everyone who speaks both remembers and thinks what he is to say; and he speaks because the will brings about that speech together with memory and thought. For whatever a man says knowingly he certainly does not say except willingly, to such an extent that whatever a man is compelled to say against his will, he does not say so long as his will is in no way inclined to speak. Hence those who now, crushed by fear or pain of temporal things, of tribulations or of torments, have abandoned the truth of the catholic faith and gone over to impiety and faithlessness, will be able to find no excuse by saying that they denied the true faith unwillingly, since it is evident that they did this by their own will. For even if the mind was brought to deny the faith by tribulation or by torment, it still did not deny it unwillingly. For in order to deny the faith it first thought and willed, and so it uttered that denial: because thought together with will decided that this should be done.
CHAPTER XVII.

To return, then, to what I was treating, in the very image of God, that is, in the very mind of man, the thought which is born and formed from the memory, and is rightly called a word, alone takes on the bodily voice, so that it can be heard by bodily ears. So too in that holy and divine Trinity, the Word of the Father alone, who is the spotless mirror and the image of God's goodness (Wis. 7:26), that is, the brightness and figure of his substance (Heb. 1:3), "though he was in the form of God, did not think it robbery to be equal with God, but emptied himself, taking the form of a servant" (Phil. 2:6). The Son alone, then, took flesh, so that he could be seen by bodily eyes and handled by hands; he alone took human nature in such a way as to make it his own, and through it mercifully to pour in the knowledge of his divinity as well. Yet in revealing himself he certainly revealed the Father too in himself. For in granting the knowledge of his divinity, he gave at the same time the knowledge of the Father as well. For the divinity which is one of the Father and the Son brings it about that neither the Son is known without the Father nor the Father without the Son. Hence he says: "Have I been with you so long, and you have not known me? Philip, whoever sees me sees the Father also" (John 14:9). So the Son, who alone took flesh, naturally shows the Father in himself by right of one divinity; just as a speaker, when he speaks a truth he remembers, shows that what he declares has been uttered by him is stored inside in his mind. But that bodily voice in which the spiritual word is clothed, so that it may be brought to the knowledge of hearers, is produced together by the memory, the thought and the will; but it is taken up by the thought alone, that is, by the inner word, so that it may go forth to the bodily ears of those standing by as a sign of the inner thought. And that word, just as, having taken on the garment of a bodily voice, it goes out wholly to the hearers, so it is found wholly in the heart, spiritually, together with memory and will. Therefore whoever has observed this image in the mind of man will the more quickly laugh at the empty talk of the heretics, who, thinking carnally about spiritual things, refuse to believe that in that holy Trinity something was made by the three which was taken up by one person only by divine disposition: whereas that human nature was made by the work of the whole Trinity, yet was taken up into unity of person by the Son alone. For just as it is certain that "In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God" (John 1:1), so it is certain that "the Word was made flesh and dwelt among us" (ibid. 14). And what do we understand [to have been made flesh]? The Lord Word, and not the God with whom the Word was; not the Father, but the Son.
CHAPTER XVIII.

So by the name 'Word' the distinct person of the Father and of the Son is shown; but because the Word was God, the one substance of the Father and the Son is taught. Not, then, of the Father nor of the Holy Spirit is that flesh which is of the Word alone: because God the Word does not have communion of one person with the Father and the Holy Spirit. For according to the common working of the divinity, in which there is a trinity of persons, as the Son made it, so did the Father and the Holy Spirit. For it was fitting that that Son who according to his divinity was naturally born alone from the Father alone should himself, according to the flesh, be naturally born of the Virgin. But in that Trinity, just as there are not two Fathers nor two Holy Spirits, so neither will there be two Sons. For that Trinity has in itself one Father, one Son, one Holy Spirit: but one Father and one Holy Spirit according to the divine nature, and one Son according to the divine and the human substance. So the Trinity is distinct in persons, although the one divinity of the Trinity is not divided or separated in nature. Therefore humanity is found taken up in the person of the Son alone. Because of the nature, then, the working of the holy Trinity is always one; but because of the persons, the taking up of humanity belongs to the Son alone. Yet while we discuss these things for the instruction of the faithful, we must also bear in mind that the heretics are carnal and natural men, and for this reason incapable of spiritual things; of such the Apostle says: "But the natural man does not perceive the things of the Spirit of God. For it is foolishness to him, and he cannot understand, because it is judged spiritually" (1 Cor. 2:14). And apostolic authority testifies that heretics above all are carnal or natural. For blessed Paul places heresies among the works of the flesh. Blessed Jude the apostle also calls those who separate themselves from the Church natural, saying: "These are the ones who separate themselves, natural men, not having the Spirit" (Jude 19). This is precisely what we have shown blessed Paul to have said: "But the natural man does not perceive the things of the Spirit of God." Let it be no wonder, then, that those who do not have the Spirit of God cannot understand divine things. For it is written in the book of Wisdom: "But who will know your mind, unless you give wisdom and send your Holy Spirit from on high?" (Wis. 9:17). Hence the holy Apostle too declares that the things of God are revealed only by the Holy Spirit, saying: "For God has revealed [them] to us through his Spirit" (1 Cor. 2:10). And a little later he says: "But we have not received the spirit of the world, but the Spirit who is from God, so that we may know the things that have been given to us by God" (ibid. 12). Nevertheless it is good that we too, so far as we are helped by God, imitating the blessed Apostle, should strive to become all things to all, so as to win all (1 Cor. 9:22).
CHAPTER XIX.

Since, then, the Arians do not grasp what we have set out, that in that one divine nature something was made by the whole Trinity which was not taken up by the whole Trinity, and it is not believed possible that the whole Trinity made that flesh which nevertheless one person of the Trinity took up, let us become, as the Apostle says (1 Thess. 2:7), like little children in their midst, and let us put before them this example, to nourish the breadth of spiritual understanding, which may neither weary nor disturb the narrowness of the heretical heart. We know that the divine Trinity alone is inseparable and indivisible, whose one nature cannot be divided by the Trinity of persons, nor can the three persons be confused by the unity of the indivisible nature. For the very mind of man, in which we have said the image of God is, received [it] in such a way that it has in itself a certain trace of the holy Trinity, yet does not have in itself a distinction of three persons. For the divine Trinity has kept this as proper to itself. Hence, although there are in the mind of man memory, understanding, and will, those are indeed three, but nevertheless they cannot be three persons: because in each man, in whose mind, or whose mind, is the divine image, there is found by nature to be one person, not only of the mind itself, but of the soul and the flesh together. Seeking, therefore, an example in the creature, so far as the greatness of so great a matter as we speak of permits, we perhaps find among natures something such as we cannot find among persons. For we have said that the whole Trinity made the humanity of the Son of God, which nevertheless not the whole Trinity, but the Son alone, received into his person. For that flesh was made by the whole Trinity, that is, by the Father, the Word, and the Holy Spirit; but the Word alone was made flesh. Since, then, as we said above, so far as the creature is concerned, we cannot find three persons in one mind, that is, in one flesh, let us at least labour to be able to find two natures in one person. For the person of each living man consists of a rational soul and a body: by which, however, many things are done in such a way that, although they are done by soul and body together, they sometimes belong to the soul alone or to the body alone. For who does not know that the body alone is refreshed and nourished by bodily food, in the eating of which there is a common operation of flesh and soul? For the soul acts through the body, or rather with the body, when the body eats; and yet the body alone receives what the soul, together with the body, acts to have received. In that eating, therefore, there is one operation of soul and flesh, but the receiving is of the flesh alone. Indeed the flesh alone is so fed by bodily food that it alone, if it has received it, grows fat. But the refreshment and fatness of the soul consists not in bodily bread but in spiritual bread. "For man does not live by bread alone, but by every word that proceeds from the mouth of God" (Matt. 4:4). Yet in the receiving of this word, so that the soul may be fed with its own food, the flesh is joined with it in the work. For this happens when the soul either applies the bodily ears to words, in order to hear, or applies the bodily eyes to writings, in order to read. See, in this too there is an operation of flesh and soul together, where the receiving is of the soul alone. Let the Arians see these things in creatures, and let them not doubt that the holy Trinity has one divine nature, and that it could happen, or rather did happen, that that flesh was made by one and inseparable work of the whole Trinity, while in the mystery of the incarnation it belonged to the person of the Only-begotten God alone.
CHAPTER XX.

So the whole Trinity did not assume flesh, nor did the whole Trinity feel the injuries of the sufferings, nor did the whole Trinity rise from the dead on the third day, nor did the whole Trinity ascend into heaven on the fortieth day; but, as I showed above, the one Son alone assumed flesh: and because in him the property of each nature remains unconfused, therefore it is one and the same [Son] who also, according to true divinity, remained wholly impassible. For that divinity by nature suffers nothing, just as by nature it is not changed. But it belongs to a changeable nature to be subject to sufferings. No suffering, therefore, could befall that nature in which natural change could not exist. The Son alone also lay in the tomb, but that nature of the Only-begotten God could be buried which could die. So according to the nature of the flesh the Only-begotten God lay buried in the rock, according to which, fastened with nails, he hung on the cross. For how could his divinity be enclosed by a tomb, which can be enclosed neither by earth nor by heaven? So the unity of person made that passion and that burial one in Christ, of divinity and flesh; but the property of each substance in Christ made the flesh of Christ alone subject by nature to passion and death, while the impassibility and immortality of the divine and unchangeable substance remained. Christ, therefore, who is not the Trinity but one person of the Trinity, thus according to the truth of the flesh truly hung on the cross and lay dead in the tomb, as the Apostle says that "Christ died for our sins according to the Scriptures, and that he was buried, and that he rose from the dead on the third day according to the Scriptures" (1 Cor. 15:3-4). All these things, which the whole Christ bore according to the unity of person, belong, according to natural property, to the truth of the flesh alone. Likewise according to the soul alone he descended to hell. For in one and the same time which is found to lie between the death of Christ and his resurrection, one and the same Christ both truly lay in the tomb according to the truth of the flesh, and truly descended into hell according to the truth of the rational soul. And therefore, according to the truth of human nature, from the moment when Christ, hanging on the cross, bowed his head and gave up the spirit, until, having received back the spirit, he rose from the dead, he was not according to the soul where he was according to the flesh. For according to the flesh he lay dead in the tomb; but according to the rational soul he descended to hell; and according to the divinity, by which he is one God with the Father and the Holy Spirit, he, the immeasurable, filled all creation. So according to the flesh he was in the tomb alone, as according to the soul he was in hell alone; but according to the divinity, by which he is enclosed by no place but is found ineffably whole everywhere (another reading: in both places), he thus did not abandon his flesh in the tomb, nor fail his soul in hell, just as he can never be absent from earth or from heaven. The same Son of God, too, who according to the flesh lay in the tomb and according to the soul alone descended into hell, since he himself had said of his soul: "I have power to lay it down, and I have power to take it up again" (John 10:18), after he laid down his soul and took it up again, ascended into heaven according to his whole humanity, and sits at the right hand of God, as Mark the evangelist testifies, saying: "The Lord Jesus, after he had spoken to them, was taken up into heaven, and sits at the right hand of God" (Mark 16:19). Now all these things which were done in time in the Only-begotten God, partly according to the soul alone, partly according to the flesh alone, and partly according to soul and flesh together, just as they are rightly referred to the one person of divinity and humanity which is in the Son of God, so they can in no way be referred to his divine substance. And therefore none of these can be ascribed to the person of the Father or of the Holy Spirit, because the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit are not one person.

Nor can anyone ascribe the passion or the assumption of flesh to the Father or to the Holy Spirit, because it is impious to proclaim the divine nature changeable or passible in any respect: according to which Christ remained always born of the Father without beginning, when he received from his mother the beginning of conception and birth; and incomprehensible, when he allowed himself to be seized; and impassible, when he felt the injuries of the passion; and immortal, when he was subject to death; and undivided, when according to the flesh he lay in the tomb and according to the soul descended into the lower parts of the earth; and immeasurable, when he ascended from the lowliness of this earth to the height of heaven.
CHAPTER XXI.

If the wretched Fastidiosus had not denied this faith, he would without doubt not be perishing. But since he denied it both by deeds and by words, it is no wonder that he became most wicked in deed, and now perverse in speech, and, walking in darkness, has shown himself an enemy of the light. For bodily fornication, which first took possession of his mind and flesh, consequently drew him to the precipice of spiritual fornication. For he took the members of Christ and made them members of a harlot. And so he did not hesitate to lose chastity of faith, because he did not grieve at having lost chastity of body. See how great an evil is lust of the flesh, which could lead that wretch even to the denial of the truth! This was, this was the storm which snatched the chaff from the Lord's threshing floor and fixed it in the briars of heretical impiety. This made him speak against his own conscience and busy himself with perverse speech to the insult of the Trinity itself. For he did not believe what he said to be true, but now with a double heart he preferred to say something other than he believed. Possessed by this despair, so that he took from himself the hope of forgiveness, he wished through licence to fulfil the delights of lust. So from his own mouth, by which he ought to have been justified, he received an increase of condemnation, when his tongue, which ought to have uttered words of penitence, uttered words of blasphemy. So the wretched Fastidiosus preferred to cross over to the place where he might both bark against God with sacrilegious insolence and, in his fornications, since he had no fear of God, not fear man either. Woe to that wretch, who wished to be deprived of the fellowship of the Church only so that he can never be free of punishment; and wished to sin without any fear only so that he might deserve to burn without end.
CHAPTER XXII.

Where now are those two years which Fastidiosus held to be happy, because, lustful, he spent them as he wished in fornication? How swiftly they passed! Even if they had been not only two hundred but two thousand, they would have passed with the same swiftness. But what will the wretch do when he comes to the judgement of him whom he denied? What will he receive for such deeds and words? What will he receive, that man, wanton in body, blind in heart, blasphemous in error? He first violated the temple of God in himself by fornication, and then went out, separated in body too from the Church. What will he receive from that holy Trinity, he who preferred to be the slave of lust and of faithlessness? What indeed but the eternal fire, which is plainly prepared for such works? And in this present time the fornication of Fastidiosus was quickly ended, yet in that fire his burning will not end but be eternal. Let Christians therefore flee both kinds of fornication into which the wretched Fastidiosus fell, so that, guarding their souls, they may keep chastity of both heart and body. Let them hold the catholic faith within the Church. Let them believe and confess the inseparable and undivided Trinity, which in its divine nature has nothing made, nothing in any way begun; by whose one and inseparable work all things were made in heaven and on earth, visible and invisible. Let them likewise believe and confess the Only-begotten God, alone born of the Father according to true divinity, alone created from the Virgin according to true humanity; and thus that flesh and a rational soul were taken up by the work of the Trinity in unity of person for the salvation of the world. Holding this most firmly, let them proclaim it and persevere in good works. For in Christ Jesus only faith avails which works through love (Gal. 5:6); whoever departs from it will be guilty of his own soul. But everyone who perseveres in it to the end, he will be saved (Matt. 10:22).
